To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the autocatalytic degradation of polylactide (PLA) is retarded by enantiomercial polymer blending.

(i) the hydrolysis of polylactide (PLA) is autocatalytic and (ii) the autocatalysis is enhanced by enantiomering of polymer blending, crystallinity, crystalline species, and molecular weight, in this order.
the in vitro hydrolyzabilities can be widely varied in the range of 0.1-1.0%/day by enantiomerc polymer blending, crystallinity, and molecular weight of PLA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the in vitro autocatlytic hydrolysis of enantiomerially blended polylactide films.
the in vitro hydrolysis behavior of the homo-crystalized enantiomerc polymer blend and the nonblended polylactide films.
the in vitro hydrolyzabilities and the molecular mechanisms of hydrolytic degradation of enantiomercrystalline PLA films.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
enantiomeric blends of polylactides are very useful in the design of PLA-based biomedical materials with a wide range of hydrolyzabilities.
the enantiomeric polymers blending and the homo-crystalling can be used as the effective means of controlling the hydrolyzability of polylactide.
the autocatalytic degradation of polylactides can be controlled by enantiomercial polymer blending, crystallinity, and molecular weight of polylactide films.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
enantiomeric blends of PLLA and/or PDLA can be designed to be hydrolytically stable or hydrolytically unstable depending upon the crystallization conditions and molecular weight.
the in vitro hydrolysis behaviors of the enantiomeric polylactide films can be controlled by enantiomering, crystalline species, and molecular weight of the films.

the autocatalytic degradation of PLA films is significantly retarded by enantiomering polymer blending and homo-crystallinity, and that the autocatalysis can be suppressed to the extent of the hydrolysis rate being almost constant for up to 2-4 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the in vitro hydrolyzabilities can be widely varied depending on the molecular structures, crystallinity, and crystalline species.
enantiomeric PLA blending and crystalline species and amount can control the hydrolyzability of PLA films.

it is possible to control the hydrolyzability of the PLA films by enantiomerial polymer blending, crystallinity, and molecular weight, and thus to obtain PLA films that have a desirable hydrolyzability for a specific application.
